> Starbie Stocks is a tiny motion-controlled desk pet that also shows live stock prices. It runs on a XIAO ESP32-C3 with an OLED, motion sensor, temperature sensor and two buttons. I designed a car-shaped PCB for it in KiCad, and I’m building it for my investing club.

### My goal

My goal is to turn Starbie into a playable character shaped like a jet or a car, with its own page for viewing real-time stocks. I'm part of an investing club, so I want a little desk device that shows the market live and is also fun to play with at school and stuff.

### 1. Learning KiCad and sketching the schematic

I learned how the pieces fit together: a schematic describes what connects to what, then you assign footprints and turn it into a physical board. I sketched the schematic for Starbie Stocks. It has:

- the XIAO ESP32-C3 as the brain
- an OLED screen and an MPU6050 motion sensor on the same I2C lines (SDA and SCL)
- a DHT11 temperature sensor with a 10k pull-up resistor
- two buttons for changing screens and tickers
- power and ground symbols, plus no-connect flags on the pins I'm not using

I checked it with KiCad's Electrical Rules Checker. I fixed power-flag warnings and a footprint library naming problem before it came out clean.

### 2. Drawing the first PCB (the original rectangle)

Next I turned the schematic into a board and drew a plain rectangular outline. I placed the parts, routed the connections as tracks on the front and back layers, and added a ground fill on both sides. This took **a lot of trial and error**. KiCad's Design Rules Checker kept finding problems, including:

- a ground connection that was too weakly attached to its pad (a thermal relief problem)
- a ground via sitting too close to a pin's drill hole
- silkscreen text overlapping pads and the board edge

Each time, I changed the layout and ran the check again until only cosmetic silkscreen warnings were left and there were 0 unconnected pads.

### 3. Using Claude as a tutor for the error fixing

One of the errors was "thermal relief connection to zone incomplete" on a ground pad. I didn't know what it meant, so I asked Claude to explain it and used the explanation to fix the layout. A thermal relief is the set of thin spokes that connects a pad to a copper fill. Mine was connecting to a tiny isolated patch of fill, so the connection was too weak. I fixed it by changing how the tracks ran so the ground pad could reach the main fill, then re-ran the checker until the error went away. I handled the via-too-close-to-a-drill-hole error the same way.

### 4. Setting up my GitHub repository

I also set up the basic GitHub repo for the project, so everything is in one place and organized:

- a folder for the **code** (the Arduino sketch)
- a folder for the **PCB** (the KiCad project and the Gerber files)
- a folder for the **images** (schematic and PCB screenshots and renders)
- a **README** explaining the project, how it works and how to build it
- a **LICENSE**
- a **BOM** listing the parts and prices

### 5. Exporting the Gerbers, coding the character and adding the BOM

- **Gerbers:** I exported the Gerber and drill files from KiCad, so the board is ready to send to a PCB fab. They're in the `PCB/gerbers` folder of the repo.
- **Code:** I coded the basic idea for a generic, talkative character, which is the starting point for the playable car or jet I want Starbie to become.
- **BOM:** I added a bill of materials to the repo with the parts I already knew I needed. The prices are still estimates, and I'll finalize them once I have the real board price, tax and shipping.

### 6. What I learned

- How footprints, nets and tracks relate to the schematic
- Why clearance rules and drill spacing matter
- How to organize a hardware project so someone else can find everything
- How to export the manufacturing files (Gerbers and drill files) a PCB fab needs
- That the first layout is rarely the final one. The rectangle doesn't fit the real, flat OLED and MPU6050 modules well, so I started redesigning it into a car-shaped board.

Next I want to turn it into a car board with a car AI character, finalize the BOM price sheet, and finish the code! :))))))))

### 2026-10-11 – ## Building the firmware, redesigning the board as a car, and reorganizing my GitHub

**6h**

## Building the firmware, redesigning the board as a car, and reorganizing my GitHub

This session took about 4 hours. I wrote the firmware, changed the whole board from a rectangle to a car shape, re-did the routing so the screen would fit, checked how it would work, and reorganized my whole GitHub repo.

### 1. Writing the code and firmware

I made the Arduino firmware for Starbie Stocks. It runs on the XIAO ESP32-C3 and keeps the original pet, tilt menu and stats screen. I added:

- a **STOCKS screen** that gets live prices over WiFi and shows the price, the daily change with an up or down arrow, and a sparkline of today's price
- a rotating watchlist of tickers, with a button to jump to the next one
- a small blinking sparkle effect next to the pet while it walks
- background WiFi downloads, so the pet and menu don't freeze while prices load

I kept the radial menu at four items and used the same pin map as the PCB, so the code matches the hardware. I renamed the sketch to `Starbie.ino` so it matches its folder, which the Arduino IDE requires.

### 2. Changing the whole board to a car

My first board was a plain rectangle. When I looked at how big the real OLED and MPU6050 modules are, I saw they lie flat and wouldn't fit around their small pin headers. So I reversed that decision and redesigned the board as a **car shape**:

- the OLED sits in the cabin, with its header on the bottom edge so the module lies flat
- the MPU6050 sits below it, and the XIAO is in the nose with its USB port at the front edge
- the two buttons sit on the hood, and the DHT11 sits between them and the screen
- the wheels are round bulges in the outline, with hub circles on the silkscreen

### 3. Rewiring the board

Moving every part meant **re-routing all the connections** (SDA, SCL, the two buttons, the DHT11 data line and 3.3V), with ground poured on both layers. I ran KiCad's Design Rules Checker on the car board and it came back with 0 errors and 0 unconnected pads. The only warnings left were cosmetic silkscreen ones.

### 4. Checking how it could work

Before exporting, I made a layout preview of the board to check how the screen, sensor and buttons sit together, and I ran automated spacing checks on the tracks and pads. This was a layout check, not a full electrical simulation, so I still need to test the real hardware once it arrives.

### 5. Reorganizing the whole GitHub

I reformatted the repository so someone else can find everything:

- the Gerber and drill files are in `PCB/gerbers`
- the KiCad project, schematic and board are in `PCB`
- the firmware is in `Firmware/Starbie`
- the screenshots and renders are in `Renders`, and the README now shows them in a gallery
- I deleted the temporary lock files and added a `.gitignore` so they don't come back
- I replaced the placeholder text in the folder READMEs
